t: Maximum Element-Sum of a Complete Subset of Indices — Squarefree Kernels
o: Select indices such that every pairwise product i*j is a perfect square, maximizing the sum of selected values. The key fact: i*j is a perfect square iff i and j have the same squarefree part (kernel). E.g., indices 1, 4, 9 all have kernel 1, and indeed 1*4, 1*9, 4*9 are squares — matching example 2's answer 20 (indices 1,4,9 hold 8+8+4). Indices 2 and 8 share kernel 2 (2*8=16), giving 7+9=16 in example 1. So group indices 1..n by kernel and take the best group sum.
k: i*j is a perfect square ⟺ i and j have equal squarefree kernels.
Compute each index's kernel by repeatedly dividing out d² for d = 2, 3, ... while d² divides the index.
Group nums-values by kernel and return the maximum group sum.

a.i: For each index i, strip all square factors: while d*d divides x, divide x by d*d, incrementing d up to sqrt(x). What remains is the squarefree kernel. Sum nums[i-1] into a hash map keyed by kernel and report the maximum entry. With n <= 1e4 this factorization loop is trivially fast.
s: Initialize an empty map kernel -> sum.
For i in 1..n: reduce x = i by removing square factors; add nums[i-1] to map[x].
a.t: O(n * sqrt(n)) — for each index, trial division up to sqrt(index).

a.i: Alternatively, iterate over squarefree bases r and stride by squares: for each r in 1..n that is itself squarefree, all indices r, 4r, 9r, ... share kernel r. Sieving which r are squarefree (marking multiples of d² as non-squarefree) then summing strides keeps the same asymptotics but avoids per-index factorization and is cache-friendlier.
s: Mark composite-squarefree candidates: for d from 2 while d*d <= n, mark all multiples of d*d as having a square factor.
For each unmarked r, accumulate nums[r*s² - 1] over s = 1, 2, ... while r*s² <= n.
a.t: O(n log n) — the harmonic-like sum over square strides per squarefree base.

w: Anchor the explanation on the kernel equivalence — it converts an opaque combinatorial condition into simple grouping. Verify with the samples: kernel 1 group {1,4,9} and kernel 2 group {2,8}. Pitfalls: indices are 1-based while arrays are 0-based, and the inner strip loop must re-check d*d <= x after divisions. Follow-up: select a subset where pairwise products are perfect cubes (group by cube-free kernel analogously), or return the actual best subset.
